turns.en: I do think one thing that was interesting about that time was for those of us who grew up and saw doom and boom firsthand. I was born and raised in the valley, so that was all around me when I was graduating high school, going to college, and then the 2008 major recession, the housing crash, the market, all that stuff. Now let's imagine you graduated college in 2009 and got a job. Well, shoot, 15 years into your career, you could be a director and you've never seen a downturn. So I think we also had, in addition to what is very unfortunately conventional misforecasting in the business that caused us to overhire and that we had to correct for, you also had a workforce that was just not at all of a mentality that this could ever happen. This felt like it was an act of God when in fact it's the cyclical nature of all businesses that this will happen at some time, and you hope it doesn't, and you wish it didn't, but you have to deal with it. Certainly, we're happy at Meta to be beyond that point, and we're growing again and executing at a stable rate and feeling really good about that. turns.en: I've failed tons of times. I've built products that nobody used. I've built technical architectures that didn't scale. I fail all kinds of times. I don't regret most of those. And so you know your main web server would put a call out over procedure call to the remote server and get a response back. And we had this really janky RPC system that I won't say who built it, but it was built and it was such a piece of garbage, constantly failing, not robust at all. And one of our best engineers, Mark Slee, built a new one called Thrift. It was a great, really great RPC infrastructure. And one of my best friends, Dave Fetterman, one of my really good friends and a brilliant engineer, we were talking about how to do the encoding and I was like, I want it to be binary encoding. I was like binary encoding, I want it to be super efficient on the wire because I'm storing these RPCs. They do two jobs for us, one of which is the active RPC, but I also stored the RPCs in a log and replayed them to do the work that we were doing in news feed ranking. That's how it was done back in the day. It was all kind of asynchronous offline. And so I wanted to be as tight as possible because my memory bandwidth was very limited and memory was so expensive back then. And Dave Fetterman was like, no no no, like that's, you know, that's term thinking, Bos. Like we should be using Linux style descriptors that are plain English language. Then you can look at the log, you can see what it is, it's parsable. Like memory bandwidth will get cheaper, but like these logs being scrutable to development is going to be a better thing. This is a totally, this is nerd bait. Those of you who've been engineers in this call, this is like Vim versus Emacs. This is nerd bait. This goes deep. This is like a long old...
turns.zh: 我失败过无数次。我构建过没人使用的产品。我构建过无法扩展的技术架构。我失败过各种情况。我不后悔大多数这些。几乎每一个我都从中学到了。你知道，那是通往更好解决方案路上的一个停靠点，或者是对这件事永远不会成功的认识，这本身就是一种礼物。所有我后悔的、我认真对待的失败，都是个人失败，我以我不自豪的方式影响了别人，也许当时不自豪，因为我无法控制自己的情绪或心情。我感到恐惧，我感到害怕。有很多这样的。有一两个突出的，我不愿意分享，因为受影响的人我认为会希望我不要分享。我会分享一个，你知道，我认为那个人现在成年了。我们有过这个非常愚蠢的讨论，我记得如此生动，在客户端-服务器架构的早期，Facebook 显然是一个网站，所以你调用服务器来获取网页，但那个服务器会调用其他服务器来收集东西。而我是远程过程调用的主要客户之一，因为 Newsfeed 排名都是在另一组服务器上完成的，那组服务器有自己的特殊需求和特殊构建以及如何组合。所以你知道你的主 Web 服务器会通过过程调用向远程服务器发出调用并得到响应。我们有一个非常简陋的 RPC 系统，我不会说是谁构建的，但它被构建了，它真是一堆垃圾，不断失败，一点也不健壮。我们最好的工程师之一 Mark Slee 构建了一个新的叫做 Thrift。它是一个伟大的、非常伟大的 RPC 基础设施。而我最好的朋友之一 Dave Fetterman，一个我非常好的朋友和一位才华横溢的工程师，我们在讨论如何进行编码，我说我想要二进制编码。我说二进制编码，我希望它在传输线上超级高效，因为我存储这些 RPC。它们为我们做两件事，一个是活跃的 RPC，但我也将 RPC 存储在日志中并重放它们来做我们在新闻 feed 排名中所做的工作。这就是当时的方式。它都是异步离线的。所以我希望尽可能紧凑，因为我的内存带宽非常有限，而且当时内存非常昂贵。而 Dave Fetterman 说，不不不，那你知道，那是术语思维，Bos。我们应该使用 Linux 风格的描述符，那是纯英语语言。然后你可以查看日志，你可以看到它是什么，它是可解析的。内存带宽会变得更便宜，但这些日志对开发的可审查性会是一件更好的事情。这完全是一个，这是书呆子诱饵。你们中那些在这次通话中当过工程师的人，这就像 Vim 对 Emacs。这是书呆子诱饵。这深入了。这就像一个漫长的老...

turns.en: Keep it coming. I like it.

A couple things: this is so and so dumb, Marley just built two encoders. It's not that hard. You just build, you pick which encoder you want for your things. That's the easiest solution ever. But also it just like it was just a it was a case where my identity was caught up in being right. Like my identity and for those who don't know identity threat is just the biggest, your worst behavior is always going to come out when you think you are under identity threat. When you feel like some core part of how you see yourself is in question, you will react with every ounce of your fiber to defend that conception of yourself because it's so expensive to reconceptualize who you are that you like defend yourself. So like my identity was being right. I got a very toss on the wrist and it caused me to take like one of my best friends, one of the best engineers I knew, a guy I literally lived with, and getting like a really embarrassing for me conflict which everyone was just like scratching their head like what is going on with Bos right now? Like I look like an unhinged crazy person. Yeah, I remember so I remember the room, I remember where I was standing in the room, I remember everything about that moment and I had to go home and be like what the was that? Like what what happened? I'm asking myself like what happened there and uh
turns.zh: 这是公司里满屋子的工程师，公司并不大，所以可能公司一半的工程师都在这个房间里，我就绝对地，我对 Dave 大喊，我 literally 脸红了，我在出汗，我对 Dave Fetterman 如此愤怒，因为他反对我的提议，而我是主要的 RPC 客户。几件事：这太愚蠢了，Marley 刚刚构建了两个编码器。没那么难。你只需构建，你为你的东西选择你想要的编码器。那是最简单的解决方案。第二件事是 Dave 是对的，顺便说一句。就像一年内，内存 definitely 不重要，相对于试图进入这些日志是多么不可理解。我不得不构建大量额外的自定义软件来解析日志并理解发生了什么。但这也只是一个情况，我的身份被卷入了正确之中。就像我的身份，对于那些不知道身份威胁的人来说，身份威胁是最大的，你最糟糕的行为总是会在你认为自己处于身份威胁下时出现。当你觉得你看待自己的某个核心部分受到质疑时，你会用尽每一丝纤维来捍卫那个自我概念，因为重新概念化你是谁是如此昂贵，以至于你会捍卫自己。所以就像我的身份是正确。我得到了一个非常轻微的惩罚，它导致我把一个我最好的朋友，我认识的最好的工程师之一，一个我 literally 住在一起的人，卷入了一场对我来说非常尴尬的冲突，每个人都只是挠头，像 Bos 现在怎么了？就像我看起来像一个失控的疯子。是的，我记得，所以我记得那个房间，我记得我在房间里站的位置，我记得那个时刻的一切，我不得不回家，像那到底是什么？就像发生了什么？我问自己，那里发生了什么，呃

turns.en: Well, in the off chance that we do end up labeling this episode 'Identity Threat', let me give you what really was. I made a lot of breakthroughs with coaching, learning about the feeling inside my own body when I was feeling that identity threat, and learning techniques and tactics to reduce the likelihood I would feel it and how to deal with it when it happened and how to repair when it did. Like I went through all that stuff. I would say the greatest lesson I learned would come years later, and it was just from observing somebody, Ami Vora, who was legendary, longtime, came in, worked on our development platform, then worked with me on ads for a long time, and then was the PM lead for WhatsApp for a long time. She's since gone on to do even more great things outside the company. Working with her was like working with, like watching, like an alien, because she and I were so different in our approach. She could have the most profound disagreement with somebody in the world, and they would say the thing that she thought was not just wrong but like crazy wrong, and she would respond, she would say, 'Fascinating, you have to tell me more about why you think that.' And I can't do it justice. She meant it like from the core of her being. She was like intensely curious. She saw this schism between her and that person, and it could have been personal, it could have been professional, it could have been anything. She saw the schism and how they saw the world, how she saw the world, and rather than reacting as if it was a threat that somebody saw it differently, or rather than reacting afraid that maybe she was wrong and had done things wrong before, she reacted with the most genuine and profound curiosity. And I just watched it absolutely tear down walls between points of view. People felt immediately her genuine heartfelt curiosity and would lean in, and that would cause them to be open-minded. And if she was right, which by the way she usually was, then they would leave being like, 'Oh, okay, I was wrong about that.' But she also would change her mind. And that was the key. I really ever since then, I just really have tried to model that. It's just reacting when I have a strong internal clench, I try to embrace curiosity. 'Wow, we do not see this thing the same way. Like, that is fascinating. Tell me why you see that.' And that could be by personal feedback. Someone's like, 'Hey, BZ, I don't think you talk enough.' 'Wow, you don't think I talk enough? That is, that's unexpected. Like, I would love to hear more about that, because no one's ever said that to me.' So I wanted to give that to anybody who might recognize this behavior in themselves. There's lots of things that you can do, and you should do that work. The work of improving yourself is always fruitful and satisfying, and it pays off as we discuss in every aspect of your life, with your family, with your friends, and professionally. This is one that I really thought was so great, was just curiosity. Embracing curiosity in those moments of challenge has really completely changed my life, and I owe that to Ami.
turns.zh: 好吧，万一我们最终把这期节目命名为“身份威胁”，让我告诉你真正的情况。我在教练指导下取得了很多突破，学会了当感到身份威胁时身体内部的感觉，并学习了减少这种感觉可能性的技巧和策略，以及当它发生时的应对方法和修复方法。就像我经历了所有这些。我想说，我学到的最伟大的教训是几年后，仅仅通过观察一个人，Ami Vora，她是传奇人物，长期在公司工作，参与了我们的开发平台，然后和我一起在广告部门工作了很长时间，之后长期担任 WhatsApp 的产品经理负责人。她后来在公司外做了更多伟大的事情。和她一起工作就像和一个外星人一起工作，因为她和我方法如此不同。她可以和世界上任何人产生最深刻的分歧，他们会说出她认为不仅错误而且疯狂错误的事情，而她会回应，她会说，‘太迷人了，你必须告诉我更多你为什么这么想。’我无法公正地描述。她是发自内心地这么说。她极度好奇。她看到了她和那个人之间的分歧，可能是个人性的，可能是专业性的，可能是任何事。她看到了分歧，以及他们如何看待世界，她如何看待世界，而不是像威胁一样反应，或者害怕自己可能错了，以前做错了事，她以最真诚和深刻的好奇心回应。我目睹它绝对地拆除了观点之间的墙。人们立刻感受到她真诚的好奇心，会倾身向前，这会导致他们思想开放。如果她是对的，顺便说一句，她通常是对的，那么他们会离开时想，‘哦，好吧，我错了。’但她也改变主意。这就是关键。从那以后，我真的试图模仿这一点。就是当我内心强烈抗拒时，我尝试拥抱好奇心。‘哇，我们对这件事的看法不同。那太迷人了。告诉我你为什么这么看。’这可能是个人反馈。有人说，‘嘿，BZ，我觉得你说得不够多。’‘哇，你觉得我说得不够多？那真是出乎意料。我很想听听更多，因为从来没人这么对我说过。’所以我想把这个给任何可能在自己身上认识到这种行为的人。有很多事情你可以做，你应该做那项工作。自我提升的工作总是富有成果和令人满意的，正如我们讨论的，它在你生活的各个方面都有回报，与家人、朋友，以及职业上。这是我真正认为很棒的一点，就是好奇心。在挑战时刻拥抱好奇心真的完全改变了我的生活，我把这归功于 Ami。

turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个最喜欢的面试问题，喜欢问你在面试的候选人？

turns.en: One of the most important things that I always ask people is: What would people who've worked with them say are their greatest strengths and weaknesses? I like this for a couple reasons, not least of which is I often do follow up with references and I like to triangulate their awareness of how other people calibrate them. And also, how they respond to criticism. Are they saying—sometimes candid surprise me—they say, 'Hey, you'll hear this critique a lot for me. I don't think it's fair.' That can be an okay answer, but they've got to be pretty robust there. Or it's like, 'Hey, this is something I'm working on. Here's what I'm working on.' But I also like to hear what they think the superpowers are. Too often a lot of attention in interview is paid to weaknesses, which I care about because I want to know what the downside is. But way more important to me is: What are you awesome at? What is the thing that if I just—I could just hitch a wagon and ride—that's what I want to know. Where's the superpower that you like it at? And what's funny is people are pretty rarely—by reference checks they're not that often accurate about what the critiques are, but they are usually pretty accurate about what their strengths are.
turns.zh: 我总会问人们的最重要问题之一是：那些曾与你共事的人会说你最大的优点和缺点是什么？我喜欢这个问题的原因有几个，尤其是因为我经常做背景调查，我喜欢交叉验证他们对自己如何被他人评价的认知。还有，他们如何回应批评。他们是否会说——有时坦率让我惊讶——他们说：‘嘿，你会经常听到这个批评。我觉得这不公平。’那可以是一个还行的答案，但他们必须相当稳健。或者像是：‘嘿，这是我正在努力改进的。这是我正在做的。’但我也喜欢听他们认为自己的超能力是什么。太多时候，面试中大量注意力放在弱点上，我关心这个是因为我想知道 downside 是什么。但对我来说更重要的是：你擅长什么？如果我能直接搭上马车骑行——那就是我想知道的。你的超能力在哪里？有趣的是，人们很少——通过背景调查，他们对批评往往不太准确，但对自己的优势通常相当准确。

turns.en: Interesting. I'm also a huge proponent of strengths and not worry too much about your weaknesses, but asking people to contextualize their performance through the team. That's so important. We do not achieve very much on our own.
turns.zh: 有趣。我也非常支持关注优势，不要太担心你的弱点，但要求人们通过团队来情境化他们的表现。那太重要了。我们靠自己成不了什么大事。

turns.en: Communication job. Yeah, amazing.
turns.zh: 沟通工作。是的，很棒。

turns.zh: 有没有一个你最近发现并喜欢的 favorite 产品？Meta 产品是可以接受的答案。

The multimodal stuff, which I'm gonna get in trouble because I've been teasing this for months on social media and it's still a closed beta. turns.zh: 好吧，这真是——我会因为这个答案惹上麻烦，因为它有点装。

turns.en: I am not a car guy, let me say that right now. I don't like cars. I don't care about cars. Like, I want a car that works and doesn't break. I grew up—all my cars growing up I had over 100,000 miles in them because we only ever had used cars. They were constantly breaking down, and like the power steering would go out while you're driving and you have to hug the thing, or the brakes would go out, or you'd throw a rod. I've done it all. So I just wanted a car. And so then I drove a Honda Accord that I bought for 10 years, and then I drove a Tesla Model S for 10 years. And a Tesla Model S had a thing happen to it while it was parked—I won't get into that. So I had to get a new car. And again, I'm like, I want to get an electric car. And I was like, I'm gonna get something nice. I'm gonna get something nice. I'm driving a Mercedes-Benz AMG EQS, and I didn't know cars could be this nice. I grew up driving used cars and like, you know, whatever. I did not know it was possible. It is the best augmented reality product I think you could buy in the market today. They have the display—it puts your turn in three-dimensional space. It's got cameras facing your eyes so it's positioned correctly on this display relative to your eyes. The turn—and so when you come up, like it's like you're hitting a little wall, you got to turn before you hit the wall. And I was like, oh my God, like I think this car is great augmented reality. So yeah, not a car guy, and I'm not trying to flex on this car or whatever it is. I like it a lot. I didn't know they could be that nice. But the thing I thought was so impressive was they did an amazing job with augmented reality in this car.
turns.zh: 我不是一个车迷，让我现在就说清楚。我不喜欢车。我不在乎车。我想要一辆能开、不坏的车。我从小到大——我所有的车都跑了超过 10 万英里，因为我们只买过二手车。它们经常坏，比如动力转向在开车时失灵，你得紧紧抱住方向盘，或者刹车失灵，或者你抛锚了。我都经历过。所以我只想要一辆车。然后我开了一辆我买的 Honda Accord 开了 10 年，然后我开了一辆 Tesla Model S 开了 10 年。Tesla Model S 在停放时出了点事——我不细说了。所以我得买辆新车。我又想，我要买辆电动车。我想，我要买辆好车。我要买辆好车。我现在开的是 Mercedes-Benz AMG EQS，我不知道车可以这么好。我从小开二手车，你知道，随便什么。我不知道这是可能的。这是我认为你今天能在市场上买到的最好的增强现实产品。他们有显示屏——它把你的转弯放在三维空间中。它有摄像头对着你的眼睛，所以它相对于你的眼睛正确定位在这个显示屏上。转弯——所以当你靠近时，就像你撞到一堵小墙，你得在撞墙前转弯。我想，天哪，我觉得这辆车是伟大的增强现实。所以是的，不是车迷，我不是想炫耀这辆车或什么的。我非常喜欢它。我不知道它们可以这么好。但我觉得最令人印象深刻的是他们在这辆车里做的增强现实非常棒。

turns.en: Wow, Mercedes-Benz, a player in augmented reality, mixed reality, big time.
turns.zh: 哇，Mercedes-Benz，增强现实、混合现实的大玩家。

turns.en: They're out there. They're out there. They're the lead.
turns.zh: 他们在那里。他们在那里。他们是领先者。

That's amazing. I'm going to have to check that out. I think we're going to increase some sales for Mercedes. Next question.
turns.zh: 我有时想举办一个比赛，赠送人们在这个环节提到的产品，现在你大大超出了我的预算。Ray-Ban Meta——你负担得起。那太棒了。我得去看看。我想我们会增加一些 Mercedes 的销量。下一个问题。

turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, think about, share with friends and family, find useful?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个最喜欢的 life motto，你经常回想、思考、与朋友和家人分享、觉得有用？

turns.en: Yeah, we have a funny—actually, how we came about this. The motto my family has—like my immediate family, like me, my wife, and kids—is just 'trust yourself.' Just 'trust yourself.' Actually, the reason we have that motto is when we have a house, we have a few nice art pieces, and one of them is a Tracy Emin—a famous UK-based artist—and she does neon pieces, and it says 'trust yourself.' And so it's in our bedroom hallway where me and all the kids and my wife are—says 'trust yourself.' And every morning the neon lights up and 'trust yourself.' And then I had the chance to have a crest made in the UK—my family's English from way back—and so we have in the crest it says 'trust yourself.' And I always talk to my kids especially. I really think people, when you're experiencing peer pressure, like who do you trust? Like them or yourself? When you're having a lot of self-doubt and uncertainty, like you have to trust yourself. I just think so much of the success I've had—I think this is probably true of most people who went to startups and succeeded—was like I just had faith that I was making good decisions. I mean, this comes back to the conviction point I made earlier about how you do things like a Newsfeed or controversial things or how you make big expensive changes—just conviction. Like you have to believe that your eyes, ears, and intellect have combined to give you a point of view that has intrinsic value and deserves your respect, as opposed to reading that newspaper article about your company and believing over what your own eyes and ears.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有一个有趣的——实际上，我们是怎么有这个的。我家的座右铭——我的直系家庭，比如我、我妻子和孩子们——就是‘相信自己’。就是‘相信自己’。实际上，我们之所以有这个座右铭，是因为我们有一栋房子，我们有一些不错的艺术品，其中一件是 Tracy Emin——一位著名的英国艺术家——她做霓虹灯作品，上面写着‘相信自己’。所以它在我们卧室的走廊里，我和所有孩子以及我妻子都在那里——写着‘相信自己’。每天早上霓虹灯亮起，‘相信自己’。然后我有机会在英国制作一个徽章——我的家族很久以前是英国人——所以我们在徽章上写着‘相信自己’。我总是和我的孩子们特别谈论这个。我真的认为，当你经历同辈压力时，你信任谁？他们还是你自己？当你有很多自我怀疑和不确定性时，你必须相信自己。我只是觉得我取得的很多成功——我想这对大多数去创业公司并成功的人来说可能都是真的——就是我只是相信我在做好的决定。我的意思是，这回到了我之前说的关于如何做像 Newsfeed 这样的事或有争议的事，或如何做大的昂贵改变——就是信念。你必须相信你的眼睛、耳朵和智力结合起来给了你一个具有内在价值的观点，值得你的尊重，而不是读那篇关于你公司的报纸文章，并相信它胜过你自己的眼睛和耳朵。

turns.en: You won't always be right and that's okay.
turns.zh: 你不会总是对的，这没关系。

turns.en: Totally, that's right. You also trusting yourself also includes taking risks because you trust that you can deal and handle with what happens when the risks don't pay out.
turns.zh: 完全正确。信任自己也包括承担风险，因为你相信自己能够应对风险没有回报时发生的事情。

turns.en: Beautiful. Final question: I know that you're an amateur photographer, maybe semi-pro photographer, a lot of travel photography. Amateur, okay. You also have this website that I came across that I don't know if people know about it. It's this funny name, I'm not going to mention it. I don't know if you want people to know. Warden short? It's an anagram of my name.
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题：我知道你是一位业余摄影师，也许半专业，拍很多旅行照片。业余，好吧。你还有一个我偶然发现的网站，不知道大家是否知道。名字很有趣，我不打算提。Warden short？那是我名字的字母重排。

turns.en: Warden short dot com. Yeah, I love photography, I love it, it's a real passion of mine.
turns.zh: Warden short.com。是的，我热爱摄影，真的热爱，这是我的真正热情所在。

turns.en: So here's the question: is there, what's your favorite photo that you've taken?
turns.zh: 所以问题是：有没有，你拍过的最喜欢的照片是哪张？

turns.en: Art is actually a great place to talk about trusting yourself, by the way. And I know it's cheesy to say it, but I think Rick Rubin's recent interviews on what art is and how people make it is spot on. You have to make it for yourself and you have to love it, and if someone else loves it and it finds broader resonance, that's awesome. But that's not always why you do it. And if you start to try to do it for broader resonance, then you're kind of chasing something else. It's media, it's entertainment, but it's not art, it's some other thing. And I say all this to basically tap dance to say I kind of love a lot of my photos. Like it's very hard to pick a favorite. The one that is popping to my head which has more emotional significance is a picture I took of my son playing in the street, just jumping in a puddle, wearing, you know, kind of a rain boot, rain slick kind of a thing. And it's not sharp, it's not in focus, it's like it's a vignette, it's an idea. And I really do think Ansel Adams talked a lot about how the goal of the photographer is to create a capture that expresses to the viewer what it felt like to be there. And people forget that he was the master of the dark room, much more even more so maybe than the capture of the print. The print was where he did amazing work. And I've had the pleasure to go to his dark room in Big Sur and spend time with his son and watch them do development in that room. And he had elaborate scripts of how he would highlight, you know, would dodge and burn different parts of the photograph to get it to have the resonance that he wanted. And he fought for photography to be accepted as an artistic medium, which it wasn't, which I find so resonant in today's AI art conversations where once again we're trying to gatekeep what is art. And you just don't get to do that, unfortunately. So this picture of my son, no one would call it a technical marvel, but as a vignette of it capturing for me personally but also I think in general for parents the ephemerality of these tremendously touching, charming human moments that you have with your children, that's the one that comes to mind.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，艺术其实是谈论信任自己的好地方。我知道这么说很老套，但我认为 Rick Rubin 最近关于什么是艺术以及人们如何创作的访谈非常精准。你必须为自己而创作，你必须热爱它，如果别人也喜欢它并引起更广泛的共鸣，那很棒。但那并不总是你创作的原因。如果你开始为了更广泛的共鸣而创作，那你就是在追逐别的东西。那是媒体，是娱乐，但不是艺术，是别的东西。我说这些基本上是为了跳踢踏舞，意思是说我有点喜欢我的很多照片。很难选出一张最喜欢的。我脑海中浮现的、更有情感意义的一张是我儿子在街上玩耍的照片，他正跳进水坑里，穿着你知道的雨靴、雨衣之类的。照片不锐利，没有对焦，就像是一个小片段，一个想法。我真的认为安塞尔·亚当斯谈过很多，摄影师的目标是创作出一张捕捉，向观众表达身临其境的感觉。人们忘了他是暗房大师，甚至可能比拍摄照片更甚。照片是他做出惊人作品的地方。我有幸去过他在大苏尔的暗房，和他的儿子共度时光，看他们在那个房间里冲洗照片。他有详细的脚本，关于如何突出，你知道，如何减淡和加深照片的不同部分，以获得他想要的共鸣。他为摄影被接受为一种艺术媒介而奋斗，当时它并不是，我觉得这在当今的 AI 艺术对话中如此共鸣，我们又一次试图把关什么是艺术。不幸的是，你就是不能那样做。所以这张我儿子的照片，没人会称它为技术奇迹，但作为一个片段，它捕捉了对我个人而言，但我也认为对父母普遍而言，与孩子共度的这些极其感人、迷人的瞬间的短暂性，那就是我想到的那张。

turns.en: Amazing. We're gonna try to find it and link folks to it. And on the point of Rick Rubin, something he says along the same lines is that you think of art as like your diary. consensus.en: Communication is the job; impact comes only through clear communication.
consensus.zh: 沟通就是工作；影响力只能通过清晰的沟通来实现。

consensus.en: Ask your leaders for help directly; they want you to succeed.
consensus.zh: 直接向你的领导者寻求帮助；他们希望你能成功。

consensus.en: Transparency and open information flow maximize talent and innovation.
consensus.zh: 透明度和开放的信息流能最大化人才和创新能力。

consensus.en: Early career: optimize for learning, try diverse roles, and embrace curiosity.
consensus.zh: 早期职业：优化学习，尝试多样化角色，拥抱好奇心。

consensus.en: Passion drives productivity; give yourself space to become passionate.
consensus.zh: 热情驱动生产力；给自己空间去培养热情。

consensus.en: Trust yourself and have conviction in your vision, even when others doubt.
consensus.zh: 相信自己，对自己的愿景有信念，即使他人怀疑。

contrarian.en: Bottom-up culture is a myth; big ideas come top-down from leaders.
contrarian.zh: 自下而上的文化是一个神话；大想法来自领导者的自上而下。

contrarian.en: Don't always listen to customers; they may reject what they'll later love.
contrarian.zh: 不要总是听从客户；他们可能会拒绝后来会喜欢的东西。

contrarian.en: Founders should sometimes delegate critical work to trusted people.
contrarian.zh: 创始人有时应该将关键工作委托给值得信赖的人。

contrarian.en: Being honest isn't enough; kindness and delivery matter more.
contrarian.zh: 仅仅诚实是不够的；善良和表达方式更重要。

contrarian.en: Apple Vision Pro isn't a breakthrough; Quest 3 is better value and features.
contrarian.zh: Apple Vision Pro并非突破；Quest 3在价值和功能上更优。

contrarian.en: Downturns are cyclical; overhiring was due to misforecasting, not just COVID.
contrarian.zh: 经济低迷是周期性的；过度招聘是由于预测错误，不仅仅是COVID。
